The roadmaps for Tau Ceti are written by humans, and are a necessarily prerequisite for developing a subject in Tau Ceti. Remember that PRs aren't accepted if they don't claim to work towards an item from an existing roadmap.

The roadmaps live at https://github.com/FormalFrontier/TauCetiRoadmap/tree/main/TauCetiRoadmap. The existing ones are just some samples that I wrote (with LLM assistance!) to seed the initial content in Tau Ceti. They are for now just markdown files, but you're welcome to experiment with Lean or markdown/Lean hybrids. (e.g. you might want to use def_wanted)

My idea for now is that all (human!) contributors to Tau Ceti can contribute to creating or updating roadmaps. Please make some PRs! I think we should have each PR reviewed by another human; PRs are merged as soon as they are approved, and as soon as you have N=2 roadmap PRs merged, you can approve roadmaps too.

I would love to see subject area experts investing some time in their roadmaps. If we can get Tau Ceti to scale, this is could be highly effective, separating the expert design work from the AI implementation work.
What is the scope of the roadmaps? Is it essentially along the lines of: everything that could conceivably end up in Mathlib one day is within scope, else it is out of scope?
No, Mathlib is not relevant here. All the mathematics that it would be good to have in a central, coordinated library, with as-high-quality-as-possible-subject-to-AI, is in scope for roadmaps.

But roadmaps have to "make contact" with the existing material in Mathlib+TauCeti. It doesn't help to write a roadmap whose "lowest rung" is still far from what has been formalized. This will just result in agents thrashing and producing terrible code.

@Michael R Douglas thanks for your roadmap PR https://github.com/FormalFrontier/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/16. Do you think you could try to rewrite it a bit so it doesn't rely on the existing external material you have? At many places, I find it hard to guess what it is asking for, but there are references to particular files in your existing material, and I worry this will hinder the AI reviewers, who might be inclined to just take your existing material as "the standard", and then accept things without sufficient adversarial review.

Simply more mathematical detail, what the definitions actually are, and ideally references to relevant freely available (arxiv?) informal sources, would help a lot. The roadmaps shouldn't just be synopses of existing external material: someone should be able to implement fresh from the roadmap, ideally.
(I would love criticism of the other existing roadmaps, from anyone here!)

Also, @Michael R Douglas, could you put some AI attribution on your roadmap PR? At least which model you used. I'm certainly using (mostly Claude) in helping write the roadmaps I've written, but the Roadmap repository, unlike the main repository, is meant to be human curated, so we should be working on the assumption that use of AI will be attributed.

I've written some further review comments on the roadmap: https://github.com/FormalFrontier/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/16#issuecomment-4751577377

The main extra comment is about library building rather than aiming at particular headline theorems.

I have another question regarding the roadmaps: I'm struggling to see the point in them. If you trust in the capabilities of the AI reviewers enough to let them judge what Lean code is good for a specific roadmap, I would have thought you would also trust them enough to make the judgment call about whether a specific PR makes a good contribution to the project, based on some general specification about in-scope content without the need for roadmaps.

If the purpose of the roadmaps is for experts to simply declare "I want to see this formalised", then I don't see why this should be baked into the review process.
Maybe to phrase my question more explicitly: What is the problem that the roadmaps, and the constraint they put on the project, trying to solve?

A few things:

  1. I want it as a barrier to entry. Everyone and their dog thinks they've uniquely discovered that AIs can write Lean code, and I don't want PRs from complete beginners driving an AI.
  2. I think that having good roadmaps really helps focus work on building a good library vs aiming for non-reusable end points (see how much better the revised version of https://github.com/FormalFrontier/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/16 is!).
  3. I hope that roadmaps will help bring people into the project, by giving them concrete things to work on, knowing that there is at least some community agreement around the value of those goals.
  4. Most importantly: I think writing good roadmaps is where human judgement / taste / "big picture" is best deployed. That library design work is where we have a comparative advantage and should be working, and I want to provide an effective outlet for people who agree and want to work in that mode.
(I will try to rewrite the Roadmap README file soon, based on the views and questions in this thread, so please jump in with criticism, views, and questions!)

Many thanks Kim! As a follow-up, it seems that there is a particular structure that the roadmaps should be in. Could it be worth standardizing that with a yaml file, similar to formalization.yaml, or do you think it is best having it more flexible?
(Naturally I'm thinking of whether this is something we could adapt for PhyslibAlpha, and the best way of doing that).

I don't want to require any shape at all on the roadmaps. I think we need to think quite soon about more formal structured metadata about the roadmaps, so we can track progress through them. But I'd prefer that this is an additional mostly-invisible-to-humans layer, and the human curated roadmaps remain flexible and unstructured.

@Michael R Douglas I'm happy with your revisions to FormalFrontier/TauCetiRoadmap#16. Claude+Codex had a few remaining suggestions, but I'll leave it up to you to decide how much (if any) of that to implement. Just ping me when you're ready and I'll merge this roadmap.

One thing that's not yet is how ambitious these should be. For example the modular curve stuff should definitely be it's own roadmap eventually, but since it links up with the modular form stuff I thought I'd mention it towards the end.

Yeah, I don't think it's helpful to "tail off" with an extremely ambitious extension, that isn't spelled out enough. It will just result in AIs trying to follow it doing stupid things. Maybe what we should do here is explicitly label these "tail" sections as roadmaps-for-roadmaps, i.e. explicitly tell contributors not to try to follow them now, but instead humans should use them as motivation for writing real roadmaps to replace them.

Michael R Douglas said:

I've reviewed this one. The big thing here is that we need to be careful about the existing WIP on the Riemann Mapping Theorem in mathlib, making sure to cite it clearly, and to ensure that we treat any RMT material in Tau Ceti as temporary shims, which will be removed once the Mathlib version is ready.

Yes Kevin commented on Riemann--Roch in my roadmap and it got me thinking, what is the process for parts of these roadmaps already on progress by someone else? Do we put a comment saying that this part will be done separately. What if we don't know someone is working on this until after the roadmap is written? I'm guessing we just update them if the people working on them have a feasible plan for the work?

It depends a lot on what they are doing.

  1. They are not aiming at Mathlib, nor a student project. Probably fine --- nice to coordinate and flag, ask if they'd be interested in reviewing the roadmaps, offer to assist or coordinate, but fine to proceed. In this case some competition and overlapping efforts is fine and healthy.
  2. If they are aiming at Mathlib. Again, probably fine, because they are aiming for something at much higher quality than here, so hopefully it shouldn't matter if Tau Ceti lands a "merely reusable" version first. But again, coordination and notification is nice, and if there's an objection to Tau Ceti proceeding on the topic before Mathlib has settled, we can probably just pause that roadmap, or cut parts out of it. But I'd prefer to instead land things, and then very promptly refactor and clean up in favour of the Mathlib version once it is ready.
  3. It's a student project. Check carefully and proactively whether they mind there being a parallel effort to get it into Tau Ceti. If they do, and they have a credible timeline for getting it done, then just steer well clear of their project here, and we'll even consider retroactively removing things from roadmaps, PRs, or merged content. (I've written a bit about this in the README yesterday.)

I've just, with @Filippo A. E. Nuccio's help, set up https://github.com/leanprover-community/project-intentions, using the new https://github.com/leanprover-community/intentions Github Action, as a proposed new place to record projects people are working on. I'm still thinking if there are ways to automatically feed information from that into our process here. This part hasn't been announced publicly yet, but I hope it will be soon, and people will use it! We'll see. :-)

@Cameron Freer, I posted a review comment on https://github.com/FormalFrontier/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/41#issuecomment-4815553701. I think we need some more outside input on this one. To the extent I can review it, it looks good (i.e. "connected to the ground" reasonably). But I need someone with more expertise on the subject area to look, too.

I think 2) is a bit more of a worry. While I agree that the mathlib version will most likely be better, if AI gets a sorry-free version before the humans working on it, I expect people would be upset since it will feel like getting scooped. Part of the fun of formalising is hitting that sorry-free milestone.
I think the project intentions looks like a really good idea. But I think the duration should have an option for PhD student, where they likely need way more than 180 days.

Yes, I hear. A few things:

  • million line formalizations of textbooks are now a thing that will appear frequently (see e.g. #AI authored projects > Erdős unit-distance counterexample, exponent above 1 today), and so people simply have to adapt to the idea that stuff is going to be done quickly and at scale
  • so we have to keep explaining and emphasising the additional value that a carefully curated / digested / reviewed formalization provides, and persuade people to value this separately from the "merely true" (that any frontier AI can produce today) and the "merely reusable" (that Tau Ceti aims for)
  • and note that I do write in a "if there's an objection to Tau Ceti proceeding" clause above, trying to allow for specific requests that Tau Ceti doesn't do something

So I agree, things have changed now that this can be done at scale. I guess I'm just pointing out that I feel that the clause should maybe be more of the default option, which would also help reinforce the additional value of the mathlib proces, since we value these projects so much that we don't really want to interrupt them (unless it's a project that's been abandoned).

Even then this isn't perfect, I expect people will be a bit put off by this, especially students and early career researchers, since they'll feel that they are "holding back" Tau Ceti by the act of taking their time to "manually" do a project.

Chris Birkbeck said:

Thanks for the review! I agree with the modular curve comments. I know it was a bit sketchy, but I wasnt sure how aspirational we wanted these roadmaps to be. I think it'll be better to remove this and then make a separate roadmap for that.

I think my main point is that (a) you don't need any representability statements to do everything else which you want to do, you just need to be able to quotient out the upper half plane by a discrete group action (in particular note that your results about dimensions of spaces of modular forms can easily be proved without even knowing what the word "functor" means, and indeed historically this is what happened) and (b) the relationship between the algebraic and analytic representable objects is subtle and I am not even sure is well-documented in the literature (although please feel free to prove me wrong; I am more confident about the claim "it was not well-documented in the literature in 1995 when I asked Brian Conrad about this").

Yeah the problem was I told Claude we'd want dimension formulas in general and I also told it we should develop things properly, so it made this weird mix with the moduli problem route, which I agree for a "grounded in mathlib" roadmap is completely crazy to have at the moment.
I still think b) is true, I struggled a lot to get my head around this and I still don't think I understand all the subtleties.
I think that if you just remove all mention of representability it should be a fine blueprint.

I do think we need to be pretty careful (i.e. much more careful than we have been so far!) in using AIs to write and review roadmaps.

I understand we want to work efficiently. But I want to try and get wide human involvement in the roadmap process, and having to read AI slop is not going to help that.

Let's set some ground rules for comments going forward: any review comments that are not human written (it's fine of course if you talk to an AI first), should be prefixed with a ":robot: model ZZZ suggests:" so it's easier to filter.

For the roadmaps themselves, I certainly don't want to forbid using AIs to help write them (indeed, I have an experiment going with a very large scale roadmap, covering ~15 graduate level textbooks on representation theory...). But we should think about how to do this better than we are so far. (No criticism, I've been using AIs to help me draft roadmaps, because I wanted to get things up quickly.)

Big fan of the :robot: suggestion.

Generally speaking, when it comes to reading text that is (co)-written by AI, I've noticed the following "metric" for myself:

  • If I suspect the prompt is shorter than the generated text, I would much prefer to read the prompt before reading the text (if at all).
  • Otoh, if I suspect that the author of the text spent more time prompting and refining this text than it will take me to read the text, then I'm much happier about reading it.

I have more questions/comments about the roadmaps and Tau Ceti in general, perhaps for when Kim is back, but I'll put them here.

  1. The description makes it sound like a roadmap is only for work we haven't yet done, but I am using it as a way to clean up work I have already done. Should it be clearer that its also fine to add work that people have completed if they write a roadmap for it? I would make sense since you might want to do the formalisation in your own repo and then once its done start adding it to Tau Ceti.
  2. Should the project also have some section on tips or useful tools to help people autoformalise maths? For example, listing things to watch out for, like crazy structures that bundle all the important bits, lots of maxheartbeat options, extremely long proofs, etc?
  3. Should there be a system where one can tag a definition or theorem statement as human verified. So that people can have more certainty that the AI didnt make a mistake on crucial bits? It wouldn't need to be exhaustive, but I think it would be a nice for headline theorems or definitions.
  4. Another question about a roadmaps ambitions: Could, for example, formalise all of EGA + SGA be a roadmap? this would start at mathlib level and definitely go way beyond the halo of mathlib or is this too much for a feasible roadmap?

Probably worth mentioning that Chris and I have been hanging out swith Akhil Mathew this week, and Akhil was asking about formalizing EGA; to him it seemed as obvious a target as Bourbaki was to Chambert-Loir, and like Chambert-Loir his idea was not the traditional "choose random targets and formalize them and see which parts of the books you need", it was "start at page 1 and continue until the end, and then stop".
I think EGA would be a great flagship autoformalisation project and one were we'd need all the tokens we can get!
The problem with EGA is that DeepMind will dump Stacks on us one day and then if we're half way through EGA then we might have a bunch of definitions twice

The problem with EGA is that DeepMind will dump Stacks on us one day and then if we're half way through EGA then we might have a bunch of definitions twice

I don't think this is a huge problem: there's no particular reason Stacks couldn't depend on Tau Ceti, or vice versa, and if there is initially overlap then it's an opportunity to improve-while-deduplicating. (Or that Stacks could be "fed into" Tau Ceti after release!) But for the most part I think it's better if we steer away from EGA in the short term, given the likelihood we'll have a lot of Stacks material independently available.

:robot: details on this from Fable 5 (edited by GPT 5.6):

PR 73 checks out completely — and more strongly than its own description claims. The decisive evidence is in the TauCeti code repo itself: TauCeti/Probability/Ergodic/ShiftInvariantSigma.lean's own docstring concedes it is the "shift-specialized form of Mathlib's MeasurableSpace.invariants; the lemmas here are only adapters", and shiftInvariantSigma is literally := MeasurableSpace.invariants (shift α). All 14 declarations are definitions, direct specializations, or short corollaries of existing Mathlib API:

TauCeti wrapper Mathlib (MeasureTheory/MeasurableSpace/Invariants.lean)
isShiftInvariant the f ⁻¹' s = s conjunct inside invariants
shiftInvariantSigma invariants (shift α) (definitional)
mem_shiftInvariantSigma_iff measurableSet_invariants (the proof is literally that lemma)
shiftInvariantSigma_le invariants_le
the two MeasurableSet.…of_shiftInvariantSigma projections the two conjuncts of measurableSet_invariants
the preimage_shift_iterate / measurable_shift_iterate group le_invariants_iterate + iterate API
measurable_shiftInvariantSigma_of_comp_shift_eq / comp_shift_eq_of_… measurable_invariants_dom / comp_eq_of_measurable_invariants

TauCetiRoadmap#72 is more complicated -- it correctly identifies a mismatch between what TauCeti has proved (about mixtures) and how it has labeled them ("conditionally IID", etc.). But in the process of changing the naming, it eliminates the conditional independence route entirely (which is proving something stronger than the mixture, and which is needed for later results about the directing random measure ν that care about it as a random variable rather than just about its law).

I'll add more details as comments and a proposed fix to the PR.
